# National Monuments Of Singapore: Al-Abrar Mosque

 By [Ng Kai](https://wonderwall.sg/search?author=Ng%20Kai&c=places--family--people--workplay--health--food)

05 February 2025

What is a [National Monument](https://wonderwall.sg/search?c=places&t=national-monuments)? Who gazettes them? How many national monuments are there in Singapore? To date, the Preservation of Sites and Monuments, a division of National Heritage Board, has identified and gazetted 77 buildings, structures and sites of national significance as an integral part of Singapore’s built heritage.

And we're here to tell you all about them - one National Monument at a time!

You've probably passed by or stepped into more than a few of them without realising they were National Monuments: [Al-Abrar Mosque](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-al-abrar-mosque), [Asian Civilisations Museum](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-asian-civilisations-museum), the [Civilian War Memorial](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-civilian-war-memorial), [St Andrew's Cathedral](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-st-andrews-cathedral), the [Esplanade Park Memorials](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-esplanade-park-memorials), [Fort Siloso](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-fort-siloso) on Sentosa - no need to plan an itinerary for friends visiting from overseas; just show them this article ✌️

In this edition, we bring into focus one of Singapore's oldest mosques, Al-Abrar Mosque.

### **📍 Location**

Al-Abrar Mosque was the 10th building to be gazetted as a National Monument in Singapore, and is located right beside other iconic National Monuments, such [Thian Hock Keng](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-thian-hock-keng-temple) temple, the[Former Keng Teck Whay Building](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-former-keng-teck-whay-building), and [Former Nagore Dargore](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-former-nagore-dargah). The MRT station nearest to it is Telok Ayer.

### 📅 Significant dates

**Dates built:**

*   1827: Began as a simple thatched hut
*   1850-1855: Construction of the present brick mosque

**Milestones:**

*   1986-1989: Underwent a series of major renovations
*   1998: Acquired a neighbouring two-storey shophouse, turned it into a _madrasah_ (a place for study) and a place for prayers

**Date gazetted:**19 Nov 1974

![Image 7](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/10/national-monuments-of-singapore-al-abrar-mosque/national_monuments_al_abrar_mosque_front.jpg?sfvrsn=590c926d_1)_IMAGE: NG KAI_

### 📜 History

Al-Abrar Mosque was established in 1827 as a simple thatched hut, which gave rise to its other Tamil name _,_(which means "Hut Mosque" in Tamil). The existing brick building was erected between 1850 and 1855. It stands on land that was originally granted a 999-year lease to Hadjee Puckery Mohamed Khatib bin Shaik Mydin as a trustee for the Tamil Muslim community.

Al-Abrar Mosque was founded in 1827, likely as a simple thatched hut, which led to its Tamil name, _Kuchu Palli_, meaning "Hut Mosque" in Tamil. The current brick structure was built between 1850 and 1855 on land granted under a 999-year lease to Hadjee Puckery Mohamed Khatib bin Shaik Mydin, who held it in trust for the Tamil Muslim community. On 21 Nov 1910, a court order was issued, under which new trustees were appointed to look after the mosque. The same trustees also looked after the[Former Nagore Dargah](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-former-nagore-dargah)on the same street, and[Jamae Mosque](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-jamae-mosque)on South Bridge Road.

Before the 1980s, the mosque underwent only minor repairs and repainting. However, major renovations between 1986 and 1989 significantly transformed its architecture.

Initially a single-storey structure, Al-Abrar Mosque underwent significant expansion with the addition of a second floor and a large jack roof to enlarge the prayer hall. The open courtyard between the entrance gate and the prayer hall was also enclosed, creating an upper gallery extension. These enhancements reportedly increased the mosque’s capacity to around 800 worshippers—more than double its previous limit. Additionally, extra space was acquired from a neighbouring shophouse and converted into a dedicated prayer hall for women.

One key figure in its development was Haji Mohamed Yusoff Hameed, who began volunteering at the mosque in 1972 and became its secretary in 1974. Presently, Al-Abrar Mosque is managed by MUIS.

![Image 8](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/10/national-monuments-of-singapore-al-abrar-mosque/national_monuments_al_abrar_mosque_exterior.jpg?sfvrsn=1b1fde70_1)_IMAGE: NG KAI_

### 📐 Design and architecture

Nestled among a row of shophouses, Al-Abrar Mosque spans the width of approximately three units and incorporates the traditional five-foot walkway at its entrance. The lot lines of the prayer hall conveniently coincide with the _qibla_ (the direction of the Kabba, the sacred building at Mecca, to which Muslims turn at prayer).

The mosque was designed in the Indo-Islamic architectural style. Its central bay is framed by two large octagonal minarets(tall towers usually attached to a mosque) topped with a crescent moon and star. These two minarets have been a visual landmark in the area since the mid-19th century.

The mosque’s merlon cresting (solid upright section of a battlement, typically of Islamic architecture) bears a resemblance to the design of [Sultan Mosque](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-sultan-mosque-hari-raya)(another National Monument) in [Kampong Glam](https://wonderwall.sg/places/adventures-at-home-lets-rediscover-kampong-glam).

![Image 9](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/10/national-monuments-of-singapore-al-abrar-mosque/national_monuments_al_abrar_mosque_inside.jpg?sfvrsn=d47acbca_1)

_IMAGE: WIKIMEDIA COMMONS/@SENGKANG_

Additionally, European Neoclassical elements bring an eclectic charm to the mosque’s design. Inside the prayer hall, Doric columns line the space, while coloured glass panels adorn the fanlights above the large French louvred windows. Above the _mihrab_(which indicates the orientation to Mecca, towards which Muslims would pray), a striking blue glass panel features a verse from the Quran in Arabic.

### 🕖 Opening hours

Regular visiting hours are weekdays from noon to 8.45pm daily. The mosque is closed on the weekend.

### 🎟️ Admission

Entry is free.

You've probably passed by or stepped into more than a few of them without realising they were National Monuments: [Al-Abrar Mosque](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-al-abrar-mosque), [Asian Civilisations Museum](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-asian-civilisations-museum), the [Civilian War Memorial](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-civilian-war-memorial), [St Andrew's Cathedral](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-st-andrews-cathedral), the [Esplanade Park Memorials](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-esplanade-park-memorials), [Fort Siloso](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-fort-siloso) on Sentosa - no need to plan an itinerary for friends visiting from overseas; just show them this article ✌️

In this edition, we explore the Former Keng Teck Whay Building,a private mutual aid Hokkien Peranakan organisation that was established almost 200 years ago.

### **📍 Location**

The building was the 58th building to be gazetted as a National Monument in Singapore, and is located a stone's throw away from the [Former Nagore Dargah](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-former-nagore-dargah). The MRT station nearest to it is Telok Ayer.

### 📅 Significant dates

**Dates built:**

*   1831: Keng Teck Whay (庆德会, or “Keng Teck Association”) was established
*   1840s: The Former Keng Teck Whay Building was built

**Milestones:**

*   2010:Ownership of the building was transferred to the Taoist Mission (Singapore)
*   2015: Reopened as Singapore Yu Huang Gong (玉皇宫, or Temple of the Heavenly Jade Emperor)

**Date gazetted:**11 Nov 2009

![Image 7: National Monument Former Keng Teck Whay Singapore Yu Huang Gong](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/10/national-monuments-of-singapore-former-keng-teck-whay-building/nm_keng_teck_whay_2026_1.jpg?sfvrsn=a12c9468_1)_IMAGE: NG KAI_

### 📜 History

**Keng Teck Association**

Keng Teck Whay (庆德会, or "Keng Teck Association") was established in 1831 by 36 Hokkien Peranakan merchants from Malacca. The men were all from distinct families, but boasted a shared lineage that could be traced back to Zhangzhou, Fujian Province, China.

Notably, one of the men was Neo Chan Guan (梁赞元), nephew to Neo Lim Kwee. The latter had built the original Hong San See on Tras Street. During the association's inception, each member contributed equally to the association's central fund, with many also supporting the construction of Thian Hock Keng Temple next door.

Keng Teck Whay was unlike the conventional clan associations, and functioned as a private family benefit society. It was the first of such organisations in Singapore, and still exists today.

With exclusive membership for the founding members and their male descendants, the association prioritises four key objectives:

*   Worshipping Sanguan Dadi (三官大帝, or "Three Emperor-Officials"); and venerating ancestral tablets of the founders
*   Providing allowances to members and their lawful wives when financial assistance was needed
*   Extending bereavement support to members and their families
*   Offering essential aid during times of need for its members and their families

![Image 8: National Monument Former Keng Teck Whay Singapore Yu Huang Gong](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/10/national-monuments-of-singapore-former-keng-teck-whay-building/nm_keng_teck_whay_2026_2.jpg?sfvrsn=6ed655de_1)_IMAGE: WIKIMEDIA COMMONS/@BJOERTVEDT_

**Singapore Yu Huang Gong**

In 2010, the ownership of the Former Keng Teck Whay Building was transferred to the Taoist Mission (Singapore). Faced with the pressing need for repair and restoration, the Taoist Mission (Singapore) undertook the transformation of the structure into a Taoist temple.

They renamed it Singapore Yu Huang Gong (玉皇宫, or Temple of the Heavenly Jade Emperor) as a tribute to Yu Huang Shang Di (玉皇上帝, or Jade Emperor), the eminent deity in Taoism. The temple warmly welcomed the public in January 2015 upon its official opening.

### 📐 Design and architecture

The Former Keng Teck Whay Building, a testament to traditional Hokkien architecture, showcases distinct features like curved roof ridges with upturned "swallow tail" sweeps, adorned with sculptures of dragons, fishes, and flowers.

Crafted using the _jian nian_ (剪粘, “cut and paste”) technique, ceramic bowls were trimmed and assembled to create intricate figures and icons. Colourful tiles embellish parts of the floors and walls.

Within the compound, three structures stand — an entrance gateway, an octagonal pagoda above a square hall, and a discreet double-storey hall at the rear. This hidden hall served as both a meeting space and an ancestral hall for members' gatherings. Enshrined within is a stone ancestral tablet bearing the names of Keng Teck Whay’s founding fathers, allowing association members to pay homage to the pioneers.

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=audpuzBdjc4)

During the Taoist Mission (Singapore)'s painstaking four-year restoration from 2010 to 2014, efforts were made to faithfully restore the building to its original design. For instance, the intricate polychromatic paintings on the temple's doors and wall panels, distinctive of the Quanzhou architectural style in Fujian province, were meticulously restored by a team of artists from the region.

The restoration team also worked on the ornamental sculptures of dragons, fishes, and flowers on the roof ridges, employing the _j_ _i_ _an nian_ (cut and paste) technique.

Regular visiting hours are from 9am to 5pm daily.

Entry is free.

# National Monuments Of Singapore: Civilian War Memorial

 By [Ng Kai](https://wonderwall.sg/search?author=Ng%20Kai&c=places--family--people--workplay--health--food)

15 February 2025

Today (15 Feb), Singapore commemorates Total Defence Day, an occasion that serves as a reminder that we must take ownership for the protection of Singapore. This year also marks the 58th anniversary of the Civilian War Memorial, a National Monument bordered by Beach Road, Bras Basah Road, Esplanade Drive, and Stamford Road.

What is a [National Monument](https://wonderwall.sg/search?c=places&t=national-monuments)? Who gazettes them? How many national monuments are there in Singapore? To date, the Preservation of Sites and Monuments, a division of National Heritage Board, has identified and gazetted 77 buildings, structures and sites of national significance as an integral part of Singapore’s built heritage.

And we're here to tell you all about them - one National Monument at a time!

You've probably passed by or stepped into more than a few of them without realising they were National Monuments: [Al-Abrar Mosque](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-al-abrar-mosque), [Asian Civilisations Museum](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-asian-civilisations-museum), the [Civilian War Memorial](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-civilian-war-memorial), [St Andrew's Cathedral](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-st-andrews-cathedral), the [Esplanade Park Memorials](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-esplanade-park-memorials), [Fort Siloso](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-fort-siloso) on Sentosa - no need to plan an itinerary for friends visiting from overseas; just show them this article ✌️

In this edition, we zero in on the first memorial in Singapore dedicated to the civilian victims of the Japanese Occupation (1942–1945), the Civilian War Memorial.

## 📍 Location

The Civilian War Memorial was the 65th structure to be gazetted as a [National Monument](https://wonderwall.sg/search?c=places&t=national-monuments), and is located near other National Monuments such as the [Esplanade Park Memorials](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-esplanade-park-memorials), [the Padang](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-the-padang), and more. The MRT stations nearest to it are Esplanade, and City Hall.

## 📅 Significant dates

### Date built:

*   1963-1967: The Civilian War Memorial was constructed

### Milestones:

*   15 Feb 1967: Every year on 15 Feb (which commemorates the Fall of Singapore to the Japanese on 15 Feb 1942), an inter-religious memorial service is held at the Civilian War Memorial. Also known as [Total Defence Day](https://wonderwall.sg/people/how-to-commemorate-total-defence-day-in-singapore), it is an occasion that serves as a reminder that we must take ownership for the protection of Singapore.
*   15 Feb 2025: The 58th anniversary of the Civilian War Memorial

**Date gazetted:** 15 Aug 2023

![Image 7: When you visit this National Monument, you're actually standing atop a gravesite. A burial chamber is housed beneath the Civilian War Memorial.](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/06/national-monuments-of-singapore-civilian-war-memorial/national_monuments_civlian_war_memorial_urn.jpg?sfvrsn=3fc2195b_1)  

_When you visit the monument, you're actually standing atop a gravesite. A burial chamber is housed beneath the Civilian War Memorial. | IMAGE: NG KAI_

## 📜 History

The Civilian War Memorial stands as a solemn reminder of the shared suffering endured by different ethnic communities and the nation’s determination to rebuild after the Japanese Occupation.

### Mass graves found post-Japanese Occupation

During excavation works in the 1950s and 1960s, mass graves containing thousands of civilian remains were uncovered across Singapore. In 1962, over 40 burial sites were found in Siglap’s _Valley of Death_. These were victims of _Operation Sook Ching_, a Japanese purge targeting anti-Japanese elements, primarily among the Chinese population. Many innocent men were arrested, taken to execution sites, and buried in unmarked graves.

![Image 8: As you ascend the steps of the Civilian War Memorial, ponder over the fact that beneath the raised platform is a vault that holds the victims' remains in 606 urns.](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/06/national-monuments-of-singapore-civilian-war-memorial/national_monuments_civilian_war_memorial_steps.jpg?sfvrsn=42b1d50d_1)  
_As you ascend the steps to the structure, ponder over the fact that beneath the raised platform is a vault that holds the victims’ remains in 606 urns. | IMAGE: NG KAI_

### Resettling the victims' remains

The Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce (SCCC, now the Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Industry) took on the task of exhuming and reinterring the victims’ remains. At the time, Singapore’s war memorials only honoured military personnel — the [Cenotaph](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-esplanade-park-memorials)(part of another National Monument) commemorated soldiers of the two World Wars, while the Kranji War Memorial paid tribute to Allied servicemen lost in the Second World War

On 19 Mar 1963, the SCCC started a Memorial Building Fund Committee to collect funds for a proposed structure, after the Government had put aside a plot of land on Beach Road for a memorial park.In addition, the SCCC matched public contributions dollar-for-dollar.

_![Image 9: The base of the Civilian War Memorial displays the words 'Memorial to the Civilian Victims of the Japanese Occupation, 1942 to 1945' in Singapore's four official languages.](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/06/national-monuments-of-singapore-civilian-war-memorial/national\_monuments\_civilian\_war\_memorial\_design.jpg?sfvrsn=19c9bd7b\_1)The base of the memorial displays the words "Memorial to the Civilian Victims of the Japanese Occupation, 1942–1945" in Singapore’s four official languages. |_ _IMAGE: NG KAI_

## 📐 Design and architecture

Design firms submitted blueprints as part of an architectural competition for the new memorial. The competition called for the winning design to express the feelings of "solemnity, tranquillity, courage and sorrow". Swan & Maclaren, the same firm that designed the Cenotaph, won the competition with their proposal of 12 parallel sets of sweeping interconnected fins forming a grand archway.

The initial winning design was later revised to become the monument we see today. Construction began in 1963, and was completed in January 1967. It was unveiled by the late Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew on 15 Feb the same year, which marked the 25th anniversary of the Fall of Singapore in 1942.

The 61m-tall structure comprises four columns, each representing one of the four ethnic groups in Singapore (Chinese, Malay, Indian, Eurasians), a reminder that regardless of race, it is imperative that we stand strong together as one Singapore in order to guard against threats to our safety and sovereignty.

## 🕗 Opening hours

It is open 24/7.

## 🎟 Admission

Entry is free.

**More than a century old, the Peranakan Museum's historic three-storey building used to house Tao Nan School (1912-1982), and then a wing of the Asian Civilisations Museum (1997-2006).** IMAGES: (CLOCKWISE FROM TOP RIGHT) FACEBOOK/@NATIONAL HERITAGE BOARD, AND NG KAI 

# Before It Was The Peranakan Museum, This National Monument Was A School

 By [Ng Kai](https://wonderwall.sg/search?author=Ng%20Kai&c=places--family--people--workplay--health--food)

30 September 2026

Today, visitors walk quietly through the Peranakan Museum's galleries filled with art and objects. Back then? I can only imagine these same corridors filled with schoolchildren running around and shouting between classes. That's because, from 1912 to 1982, this beautifully restored [National Monument](https://wonderwall.sg/search?c=places&t=national-monuments) on Armenian Street was Tao Nan School, which feels especially apt with Children’s Day (2 Oct) coming up.

## Overview

*   **Official name:**Former Tao Nan School, now the Peranakan Museum
*   **Address:**[39 Armenian Street, Singapore 179941](https://maps.app.goo.gl/WyLzBZcV2rMjs7AV8)
*   **Built:**1910-1912
*   **Original use:**Tao Nan School
*   **Former use:**[Asian Civilisations Museum](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-singapore-asian-civilisations-museum)
*   **Current use:** Peranakan Museum
*   **Year gazetted as a National Monument:** 1998
*   **Nearest MRT station:**Bras Basah
*   **Admission:**Permanent galleries are [free](https://www.peranakanmuseum.nhb.gov.sg/visit/plan-your-visit) for Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents
*   **Opening hours:**10am-7pm daily; till 9pm on Fridays

## Why the Peranakan Museum is worth a visit

Even before you step inside, the building is already photogenic. There’s the symmetrical facade, rows of arched windows and columns, spacious verandahs and that bright central atrium inside.

As for all the spaces filled with art displays today? The galleries were once classrooms; the ground floor was the assembly hall, and the canteen and kitchen sat behind the building.

Museum etiquette asks visitors to keep their voices low and avoid running in the galleries. But decades ago, those same spaces were probably filled with children doing exactly the opposite (just picture the mayhem).

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zXDHc3tdBC4)

## The origins of Tao Nan School

Chen Baochen (陈宝琛), a tutor of the last Qing emperor, was credited for naming the school _Dao Nan Xue Tang_ (道南学堂, or Tao Nan School). The name _Dao Nan_ was derived from the phrase _wu dao qi nan_ (吾道其南), which can be loosely translated as "My code of behaviour is promulgated in Southeast Asia".

The first Tao Nan School was situated opposite [Saint Andrew’s Cathedral](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-st-andrews-cathedral) in Siam House, the residence of Tan Kim Ching (陈金钟), the son of Tan Tock Seng. With an increasing enrolment, the rented Siam House was near its maximum capacity. The school leaders decided that it was necessary to erect a proper building for Tao Nan School.

The sugar baron Oei Tiong Ham (黄仲涵) gifted a sizeable sum for the purchase of the plot of land at Armenian Street. Among those who donated to setting up Tao Nan School were prominent Chinese merchants, including Low Kim Pong (刘金榜, who built [Lian Shan Shuang Lin Monastery](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-lian-shan-shuang-lin-monastery)) and Tan Kah Kee (陈嘉庚, who founded [The Chinese High School)](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-hwa-chong-chinese-high-school-clock-tower-building).

The school building was completed in March 1912 and stayed on its premises for close to 70 years. In 1982, Tao Nan School moved to its new campus in Marine Parade, where it remains today.

![Image 7: Asian Civilisations Museum (ACM)'s first opening at Armenian Street in 1997.](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/06/national-monuments-of-singapore-asian-civilisations-museum/national_monuments_asian_civilisations_museum_opening_1997_1.jpg?sfvrsn=2455561a_1)  
_ACM's first opening at Armenian Street in 1997. | IMAGE COURTESY OF ASIAN CIVILISATIONS MUSEUM_

![Image 8: The opening of Asian Civilisations Museum (ACM) in 1997 was graced by Mr Lee Hsien Loong, who was then the Deputy Prime Minister of Singapore.](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/06/national-monuments-of-singapore-asian-civilisations-museum/national_monuments_asian_civilisations_museum_opening_1997_2.jpg?sfvrsn=120b2b46_1)  
_The opening in 1997 was graced by Mr Lee Hsien Loong (middle), who was then the Deputy Prime Minister of Singapore. | IMAGE COURTESY OF ASIAN CIVILISATIONS MUSEUM_

## From school to the first museum iteration

The original school building at Armenian Street was later refurbished as the [Asian Civilisations Museum (ACM)](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-asian-civilisations-museum), which opened to the public on 21 Apr 1997. From 2006-2008, the building underwent redevelopment to house the world’s first Peranakan Museum, which officially opened to the public on 25 Apr 2008.

It closed again for a major revamp in 2019 before [reopening in Feb 2023](https://wonderwall.sg/places/peranakan-museum-reopens) after four years of renovation (delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic). The museum explores the culture of Peranakan communities in Southeast Asia, and possesses one of the finest and most comprehensive public collections of Peranakan objects.

![Image 9: National Monument Peranakan Museum Singapore](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/12/national-monuments-of-singapore-peranakan-museum/nm_peranakan_museum_2026_10.jpg?sfvrsn=92a671a5_1)

![Image 10: National Monument Peranakan Museum Singapore](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/12/national-monuments-of-singapore-peranakan-museum/nm_peranakan_museum_2026_11.jpg?sfvrsn=8743ed64_1)_IMAGES: NG KAI_

Displaying over 800 articles (ranging from newly acquired or generously donated items to well-loved artefacts and set pieces), the museum explores the Peranakan identity through universal themes of “Origins”, “Home”, and “Style”.

If you think about it, the current Peranakan Museum and ACM have effectively swapped historic buildings over the years, almost like museum musical chairs.

## What to look out for when you visit

![Image 11: National_Monument_Peranakan_Museum_Ground_Floor](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/12/national-monuments-of-singapore-peranakan-museum/national_monument_peranakan_museum_ground_floor.jpg?sfvrsn=510e6191_1)  
_The view from the ground floor. | IMAGE: NG KAI_

![Image 12: National_Monument_Peranakan_Museum_Second_Floor](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/12/national-monuments-of-singapore-peranakan-museum/national_monument_peranakan_museum_second_floor.jpg?sfvrsn=f4ff3d8e_1)  
_The view from the second floor. | IMAGE: NG KAI_

![Image 13: National Monument Peranakan Museum Singapore](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/12/national-monuments-of-singapore-peranakan-museum/nm_peranakan_museum_7.jpg?sfvrsn=f8fd8be7_1)_The view from the third and highest floor. | IMAGE: NG KAI_

### The spaces that used to be classrooms

One detail that changed my perspective of the museum? The rooms surrounding the central atrium weren’t originally designed to display jewellery, textiles and ceramics - they were classrooms. The assembly hall occupied the ground floor, while students had lessons across all three levels.

It made me wonder what this place would've been like if the students back then had social media. With those arched windows, grand staircases and that magnificent facade, the school-day photo dumps would’ve levelled up. Every recess period would see someone taking photos somewhere.

![Image 14: Cast-iron eagles atop the entrance of Peranakan Museum, the former Tao Nan School](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/12/national-monuments-of-singapore-peranakan-museum/nm_peranakan_museum_2026_9.jpg?sfvrsn=51249f7b_1)

![Image 15: Cast-iron eagle atop the entrance of Peranakan Museum, the former Tao Nan School](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/12/national-monuments-of-singapore-peranakan-museum/nm_peranakan_museum_2026_2.jpg?sfvrsn=208d3ba7_1)_IMAGES: NG KAI_

### Look out for two huge eagles outside

I initially assumed the pair of cast-iron eagles at the entrance were simply decorative. But they’re actually surviving pieces of Tao Nan School, each weighing around 200kg.

There are different theories about what they symbolise: some presume they were installed to ward off evil, while others believe they represent the excellence which Tao Nan School strives for, as the character _ying_ (英) in the term _jing ying_ (精英) – which means "cream of the crop" – is a homophone of _ying_ (鹰), or "eagle".

When Tao Nan School moved to Marine Parade in 1982, the two eagle sculptures were brought to its new premises. However, in 1996, the sculptures were returned to the newly restored former building and reinstated in their original locations on the gate posts.

Lowkey, the school moved on, but two of its most recognisable “students” eventually came home.

![Image 16: National_Monument_Peranakan_Museum_Facade](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/12/national-monuments-of-singapore-peranakan-museum/national_monument_peranakan_museum_facade.jpg?sfvrsn=c9861f91_1)_IMAGE: NG KAI_

### The Neoclassical facade

Designed by the Municipal Engineer’s Office of Singapore, the former Tao Nan School’s architecture is eclectic.

Neoclassical elements are featured on the building’s facade, and include ornate Corinthian capitals atop the many fluted columns (those with shallow grooves) and pilasters (rectangular columns). The building also exhibits various tropical adaptations, including spacious verandas and large windows that allowed the edifice to be naturally ventilated before air-conditioning was finally installed.

## Thinking of Children's Day plans for your kids?

The Peranakan Museum is a pretty fitting place for a kid-friendly outing. There’s the [Anak Anak Storytelling Guide](https://www.peranakanmuseum.nhb.gov.sg/learn/digital-resources/anak-anak-storytelling-guide), a free self-guided experience for children aged four and above. Kids can scan QR codes around the galleries to hear stories inspired by objects such as an _ang ku kueh_ mould, a beaded lion and a first-birthday tradition, with an activity trail to follow along.

There’s a nostalgic full-circle moment here, too. More than a century after Tao Nan students first started their schooling journey inside this building, children are still coming here to learn.

* * *

## Wait, what makes something a National Monument?

In Singapore, [National Monuments](https://wonderwall.sg/search?c=places&t=national-monuments) are buildings, structures or sites recognised for their national significance and value to our built heritage. They are gazetted by the Preservation of Sites and Monuments, a division of the National Heritage Board, which is why the title is reserved for places that carry especially important historical, architectural, social or cultural meaning.

As of 2026, Singapore has 77 National Monuments. Some are obvious landmarks, like the [Padang](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-the-padang), [St Andrew’s Cathedral](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-st-andrews-cathedral) and [Fort Siloso](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-fort-siloso). Others are places you may have walked past without a second thought, which is exactly why this series exists.

One [National Monument](https://wonderwall.sg/search?c=places&t=national-monuments) at a time, we’re here to uncover the stories hiding in plain sight.

##### Art

### [Step into the worlds of Van Gogh, Monet and Gustav Klimt at this 360-degree art experience at Parkview Square](https://www.timeout.com/singapore/news/step-into-the-worlds-of-van-gogh-monet-and-gustav-klimt-at-this-360-degree-art-experience-at-parkview-square-011025)

You might have heard about Monet Inside, an immersive art exhibition that opened last year, allowing visitors to step into 200 of famous painter Claude Monet's dreamy paintings. If that sounds like your vibe, or if you’ve already been there and done that, here’s the deal: the 360-degree art experience has now added two more classic iconic artists to their show: Gustav Klimt, and Vincent van Gogh, from January 24, 2025. Presented by Groundseesaw at Parkview Square, the event features stunning visuals, original soundtracks, and captivating storytelling showcased across the venue's floors and five towering screens, each exceeding six meters in height. Photograph: GroundseesawGustav Klimt If Gustav Klimt rings a bell, you’ll surely recognise his iconic masterpiece, The Kiss. This celebrated painting will be transformed into a digital projection, allowing you to get up close to its intricate details. Paired with lyrical music and mesmerizing visuals, Klimt’s exploration of beauty, love, and the human experience is brought to life in an emotionally captivating way. Moreover, a dedicated narrator will bring Klimt’s world to life, sharing vivid tales of his artistic vision, personal challenges, and the cultural influences that shaped his work. Photograph: GroundseesawVincent van Gogh For Van Gogh, 11 original orchestral soundtracks and breathtaking digital projections will come into play, featuring famous pieces such as Starry Night and Sunflowers in vivid detail. Similarly, a narrator will guide you through an evocative journey to 19th-century Netherlands and France, shedding light on Van Gogh's struggles, inspirations, and remarkable creativity. Each experience includes 45 minutes of storytelling through video and 15 minutes to explore the space and capture photos. Factoring in time to visit the art shop and tour the exhibition hall, the entire experience takes approximately 1 hour and 30 minutes. Separate tickets are required for each of the three shows. Ticket sales will commence from January 9, 2025, and can be purchased via Groundseesaw’s page here. HAVE YOU HEARD? ### [The exclusive Louis Vuitton x Murakami Pop-Up lands in Joo Chiat, Singapore – the only one in Southeast Asia](https://www.timeout.com/singapore/news/the-exclusive-louis-vuitton-x-murakami-pop-up-lands-in-joo-chiat-singapore-the-only-one-in-southeast-asia-010325)

Ever come across a psychedelic flower motif with a smiley face? That’s most likely the iconic symbol of one of Japan’s most celebrated artists, Takashi Murakami. Known for his vibrant, playful motifs like the smiling flower and a vibrant ‘superflat aesthetic’, Murakami's work spans fine art, fashion, and commercial collaborations. Photograph: Daniel Iskandar Among his standout collaborations is his legendary partnership with fashion house Louis Vuitton. First launched in 2003, this creative fusion now celebrates its 20th anniversary with an extensive re-edition collection of more than 200 creations. Photograph: Daniel Iskandar And lucky us, because Singapore gets the spotlight as Southeast Asia’s exclusive host for the Louis Vuitton x Murakami pop-up, happening at 72 Joo Chiat Place from January 4 to 19, 2025. Other cities in which the pop-up will be activated include London, Milan, Tokyo, New York, Shanghai and Seoul. Photograph: Daniel IskandarLouis Vuitton x Murakami Pop-up at Joo Chiat Visitors to the pop-up will be greeted by Takashi Murakami’s iconic smiling flower sculptures, also known as the 3D Superflat Garden, at the entrance. # National Monuments Of Singapore: Sri Thendayuthapani Temple

 By [Ng Kai](https://wonderwall.sg/search?author=Ng%20Kai&c=places--family--people--workplay--health--food)

29 May 2024

What is a [National Monument](https://wonderwall.sg/search?c=places&t=national-monuments)? Who gazettes them? How many national monuments are there in Singapore? To date, the Preservation of Sites and Monuments, a division of National Heritage Board, has identified and gazetted 77 buildings, structures and sites of national significance as an integral part of Singapore’s built heritage.

And we're here to tell you all about them - one National Monument at a time!

You've probably passed by or stepped into more than a few of them without realising they were National Monuments: [Al-Abrar Mosque](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-al-abrar-mosque), [Asian Civilisations Museum](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-asian-civilisations-museum), the [Civilian War Memorial](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-civilian-war-memorial), [St Andrew's Cathedral](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-st-andrews-cathedral), the [Esplanade Park Memorials](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-esplanade-park-memorials), [Fort Siloso](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-fort-siloso) on Sentosa - no need to plan an itinerary for friends visiting from overseas; just show them this article ✌️

In this edition, we highlight one of Singapore's oldest Hindu temples, Sri Thendayuthapani Temple.

## 📍 Location

Sri Thendayuthapani Temple was the 67th building to be gazetted as a National Monument, and is located near other National Monuments such as [Hong San See](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-hong-san-see) and [Chesed-El Synagogue](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-chesed-el-synagogue). The MRT stations nearest to it are Fort Canning and Dhoby Ghaut.

## 📅 Significant dates

**Date built:**

*   4 Apr 1859: Sri Thendayuthapani Temple was built

**Milestones:**

*   Late 1970s: The temple began reconstruction at the same site; the multi-million project was funded by the Chettiar community
*   1983: Reconstruction was completed, and the temple was consecrated on 24 Nov the same year
*   27 Nov 2009: The temple was reconsecrated

**Date gazetted:**20 Oct 2014

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=orZ_kRPLFFo)

## 📜 History

Originating from the Chettinad region in Tamil Nadu, the Nattukottai Chettiars (also known as Nagarathars) were among the first immigrants to settle in Singapore. The Chettiars, who came to Singapore in the early 19th century, were traders, merchant bankers, and financiers. A large majority of them often based their economic and religious activities around the South-Indian-style Sri Thendayuthapani Temple, also known as the Chettiars' Temple.

![Image 7: A traditional Chettiar kittangi comprising a father and son duo, circa 1920.](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2024/05/national-monuments-of-singapore-sri-thendayuthapani-temple/national_monuments_sri_then_temple_kittangi.jpg?sfvrsn=6600a509_1)_A traditional Chettiar "kittangi" comprising a father and son duo, circa 1920. |_ _IMAGE: WIKIMEDIA COMMONS/@ HARI147_

Once the Chettiars had established themselves as the main Indian merchant-banking community in the city, many of them operated moneylending businesses, known as _kittangis_, along Market Street and Tank Road.

Traditionally, the Chettiars are followers of Shaivism, the Hindu sect that venerates Shiva (the father of Murugan) as the supreme deity. Even after leaving Chettinad for various parts of Asia in the 19th century, they maintained their tradition of building temples dedicated to Murugan in their new settlements.

In 1859, the Chettiar community constructed the Sri Thendayuthapani Temple on Tank Road.The Chettiar community had purchased the land for the current temple from the estate of Thomas Oxley, Singapore's first Surgeon General. Initially, the temple was a simple structure.

At the entrance, there were two raised platforms typical of Chettiar households in Tamil Nadu, India. It featured an _alangara mandapam_ and an _artha mandapam_. The _alangara mandapam_ was used to display decorated deities during special occasions, while the _artha mandapam_ served as the central hall leading to the main sanctum.

![Image 8: The gopuram or entrance tower at Sri Thendayuthapani Temple in 1995.](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2024/05/national-monuments-of-singapore-sri-thendayuthapani-temple/national_monuments_sri_then_temple_1995.jpg?sfvrsn=8bd1fe22_1)_The "gopuram" or entrance tower in 1995. |_ _IMAGE: WIKIMEDIA COMMONS/@MIKELYNCH._

While primarily serving as a religious institution, the Sri Thendayuthapani Temple also functioned as a social and commercial hub for the Chettiar community. Each Chettiar firm voluntarily contributed to the temple. In 1928, the Nattukottai Chettiars’ Chamber of Commerce was established within the temple grounds. Historically, business transactions were conducted before the statue of Murugan, seeking his blessings and presence to witness the deals.

Over 60 years later, in 1925, the Chettiars established the Sri Layan Sithi Vinayagar Temple on Keong Saik Road in Chinatown, where Ganesha, Murugan’s brother, is the main deity. Today, both temples are overseen by the Chettiars’ Temple Society.

[Video 2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eb8SOAWGfXE)

Sri Thendayuthapani Temple has been closely linked with [Thaipusam](https://wonderwall.sg/people/things-you-never-knew-about-thaipusam), a major festival celebrated by Tamil Hindus, especially the Chettiars, to honour Murugan for his victory over evil. Murugan symbolises youth, power, and virtue, and is revered as the clan deity of the Chettiars, the patron deity of Tamils, and the Hindu god of righteousness.

The annual Thaipusam celebration is marked by grand processions. On the eve of Thaipusam, Murugan’s statue is placed in a silver chariot and taken on a procession through the city to Sri Layan Sithi Vinayagar Temple, then returned to Sri Thendayuthapani Temple in the evening. This procession, known as _Punar Pusam_ or _Chetty Pusam_, attracts a crowd comprising mostly of the Chettiar community.

A bigger, more extravagant procession occurs on the festival day itself. Thousands of Hindu and non-Hindu devotees gather at Sri Srinivasa Perumal Temple on Serangoon Road to participate in a 3km procession ending at Sri Thendayuthapani Temple, where the devotees are warmly received.

> [View this post on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/p/CogJOM5PSk9/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)
> [A post shared by atina (@indietrekkr)](https://www.instagram.com/p/CogJOM5PSk9/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)

During the procession, many men carry _kavadis_, elaborately decorated steel structures, as acts of penance or in gratitude for answered prayers. The _kavadis_ are adorned with peacock feathers as the peacock is symbolic of Murugan’s _vahana_ (divine vehicle).

Other devotees carry _paal kudams_ (milk pots) on their heads. Before World War II, the event would end with grand fireworks display at the [Padang](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-the-padang).

> [View this post on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/p/wQK-UpC_SC/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)
> [A post shared by Kenneth Pinto (@acroamatic)](https://www.instagram.com/p/wQK-UpC_SC/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)

Today, other than the annual Thaipusam festival, the temple offers a variety of programmes, including walk-a-jogs, and the tradition of providing _annathaanam_ (free food) during special occasions for all attendees.

Couples can also marry in the Chettiar Wedding Hall, a space specifically constructed for the community to conduct traditional wedding ceremonies.

## 📐 Design and architecture

Originally built as a private temple for the Chettiar community, Sri Thendayuthapani Temple opened its doors to other Hindus from the broader Indian community over time. In the late 1970s, the temple committee decided to reconstruct the temple, with the Chettiar community funding the reconstruction cost.

The temple was consecrated on 24 Nov 1983; the affair attended by notable guests including former President of Singapore Mr. C. V. Devan Nair, Mrs. Devan Nair, and Members of Parliament.

> [View this post on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/p/C7LNivISImU/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)
> [A post shared by Angelina 🇺🇦 ➡️ 🇦🇺 (@slivki82)](https://www.instagram.com/p/C7LNivISImU/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)

Designed in the South Indian architectural style, Sri Thendayuthapani Temple's five-tiered _gopuram_ (entrance tower) was among the tallest and most impressive in Southeast Asia when completed. The gopuram allows devotees to view the temple from a distance and offer prayers if they cannot visit the temple. It is adorned with statues of Hindu deities, including various forms of Shiva and Murugan.

![Image 9: The Sri Thendayuthapani Temple showcases elements commonly found in Chettiar architecture, such as the thinnais (raised platforms) at the entrance and glass panels in the clerestory of the mandapam (prayer hall).](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2024/05/national-monuments-of-singapore-sri-thendayuthapani-temple/national_monuments_sri_then_temple_inside.jpg?sfvrsn=3573cfb5_1)_IMAGE: WIKIMEDIA COMMONS/@SHESMAX_

The temple showcases elements commonly found in Chettiar architecture, such as the _thinnais_ (raised platforms) at the entrance and glass panels in the clerestory of the _mandapam_ (prayer hall). _Thinnais_ are usually added on either side of the main entrances in Chettinad homes as seating areas for family members and visitors.

Glass panels in Chettiar temples often feature engravings of Hindu deities. In Sri Thendayuthapani Temple, the 48 glass panels depict the various forms of Shiva’s mystical dance, the Nataraja (Lord of the Dance), and different forms of Ganesha, among other Hindu deities.

The temple underwent another round of restoration in the late 2000s, in keeping with the Hindu tradition of renewing temples every 12 years. It was reconsecrated on 27 Nov 2009.

## 🕖 Opening hours

Regular visiting hours are daily, from 7am to 12pm and 5.30pm to 8.30pm.

## 🎟️ Admission

Entry is free. Do observe appropriate dressing and decorum. Find out more [here](https://sttemple.com/plan-a-visit/).

# The ultimate guide to Jalan Besar

There's more to do in this foodie wonderland than restaurant and café-hopping

Jalan Besar literally translates to 'big road'. How big is the neighbourhood, you ask? Jalan Besar is a tale of two former swamps – one by the Rochor River and the other by the Kallang River. Stretching between two points, this neighbourhood has long been filled with hardware suppliers, auto garages, canvas suppliers, and lighting wholesalers.

Since its urbanisation in the late 1800s, wallet-friendly restaurants have moved in to cater to immigrant workers and labourers. Zoom to the present, and you'll find that many of these traditional eateries are still standing – alongside a contemporary crop of [restaurants](https://www.timeout.com/singapore/restaurants/the-50-best-restaurants-in-singapore), [bars](https://www.timeout.com/singapore/bars-and-pubs/best-bars-in-singapore),[cafés](https://www.timeout.com/singapore/restaurants/best-cafes-in-singapore), and [cool shops](https://www.timeout.com/singapore/shopping/the-best-shops-in-singapore). Some have been here for at least a decade themselves – take third-wave coffee pioneer Chye Seng Huat Hardware and craft beer bar Druggists –with even newer entrants like a circular fashion hub, gallery dedicated to textiles, and soon, a co-living space for creatives.

The result is – as with most of Singapore's coolest neighbourhoods – a charming mix of old and new. Here, it feels real, unplanned, and organic, and it takes a proper wander to develop a good appreciation of the neighbourhood. So, to get you started on your exploration,here are some of the best things to see, do, eat and drink in Jalan Besar.

## DO

### 1.Petain Street shophouses

![Image 5: Petain Street shophouses](https://media.timeout.com/images/106447596/750/422/image.jpg)

![Image 6: Petain Street shophouses](https://media.timeout.com/images/106447596/750/562/image.jpg)

Photograph: Jon LC

Bring your camera along to Petain Street – you’ll need it. These shophouses are a stunning masterclass in Singapore’s Chinese Baroque architectural style, featuring intricate ceramic tiles, relief plasterwork, and charming pink and pistachio-green facades. Built in the early 1930s by architect E.V. Miller for landlord Mohamed bin Haji Oma, these 18 shophouses have survived threats of demolition in the 1970s and 1980s, and were finally conserved under the Jalan Besar Conservation Act in 1991. Today, they’re private homes for some very lucky residents – so observe from afar and take your pictures discreetly.

### [2.Jalan Besar Stadium](https://www.timeout.com/singapore/sport-and-fitness/jalan-besar-stadium)

If there was one place we’d call the home of Singapore football, it’d be Jalan Besar Stadium. This 6,000-seat venue has hosted legendary Malaysia Cup clashes and international fixtures since 1929, and is today the homeground of the Singapore Premier League club Young Lions and Lion City Sailors – the Singapore National Team also frequently uses this stadium when the National Stadium is booked out for major events. You can still catch local and regional games there like the ASEAN Championship.

Photograph: @jaxtonjx/Instagram

Take a slow stroll down Tyrwhitt Road to catch vivid street art hidden down side alleys and shophouse walls. Some highlights include Jaxton Su’s Chicken Pie vs. Crab mural on 43 Tyrwhitt Road, a playful work depicting a battle between kopitiam uncles as onlookers watch and record. You’ll also find rotating street art on the side of Chye Seng Huat Hardware – it has featured past pieces by artists like Mike Herabot and Julie Chua.

### 4.aNERDgallery

Singapore’s first gallery dedicated exclusively to Indonesian textile art, aNERDgallery will change how you view regional craft. Founder Tony Sugiarta works directly with Southeast Asian artisans and researchers to showcase batik (wax-resist dyeing) and tenun (handwoven fabric) as vibrant, contemporary art forms. Drop by to browse striking textile exhibitions, attend intimate artist talks, or join hands-on workshops that give Nusantara heritage a decidedly modern edge.

This one’s, well, quite the hidden gem. Singapore’s first private gem museum offers a curious peek into the journey of precious stones from mine to market. Here, you can explore raw mineral specimens, learn the science behind gemology, and admire rare, polished stones tucked away on the upper floor of the shophouse. It’s a quick but charming diversion for whenever you’re in Jalan Besar.

Admission is free, but you must register before visiting as the museum does not accept walk-ins. If you prefer a guide, The Gem Museum offers private tours on Tuesdays and Thursday, 2pm to 3pm.

Swee Choon Dim Sum is an undisputed late-night rite of passage in Singapore. This spot has been fuelling partygoers and night owls with handmade dim sums since 1962, but you’re welcome to pull up as early as 7am for a hot bowl of porridge. Either way, don’t leave without ordering the signature mee suah kueh, the prawn and banana fritter, beancurd prawn roll, and salted egg yolk custard bun. They do classics like har gaw and siew mai well, too. For something more filling, try the hor fun or fried rice – pair with a side of HK milk tea and you’ve completed the experience.

### 2.Berseh Food Centre

![Image 20: Berseh Food Centre](https://media.timeout.com/images/106447599/750/562/image.jpg)

Photograph: Daniel Ferryanto/Shutterstock

This two-storey hawker centre remains one of Singapore’s best-kept secrets for great local food. Popular with the older crowd, this spot is famous for some pretty exotic foods: think turtle soup, crocodile meat, and pig trotter jelly. But there’s good stuff that’s more approachable, like the crispy oyster cakes at Fu Zhou Poh Hwa, stuffed epok epok (traditional Malay deep-fried pastries) at Epok Epok Story, savoury mutton soup from Jalan Besar Mutton Soup, and fluffy ice kachang at Hot & Cold Dessert Store.

### 3.Ming Chung Restaurant

![Image 21: Ming Chung Restaurant](https://media.timeout.com/images/106447598/750/422/image.jpg)

![Image 22: Ming Chung Restaurant](https://media.timeout.com/images/106447598/750/562/image.jpg)

Photograph: Ming Chung Restaurant

This old-school institution has been serving up Henghwa cuisine since 1933, serving rickshaw riders, labourers, and Henghwa immigrants a taste of home at affordable prices. Now run by the third generation, Ming Chung continues to serve home-style Henghwa dishes, which are lighter, milder, and more seafood-focused compared to the dark, savoury sauces and braised foods in Hokkien cuisine.

A great example is Ming Chung’s famous lor mee, featuring handmade noodles in a white broth and laden with seafood, pork, yam and vegetables. Other must-tries are the fried mee sua (stir-fried vermicelli with seafood, pork, seaweed, and peanuts), fried batang fish, and stir-fried nian gao.

This one’s a paradise for cheese lovers. The Cheeselads is a cosy artisanal cheese shop on Tyrwhitt Road serving up cheese platters, charcuterie boards, and sharing plates paired with curated wines. If you’re here to graze, your best bet is the Cheesemonger’s Choice, the restaurant’s signature platter laden with a rotating selection of five cheeses, nuts, and nougats. Otherwise, try its signature truffle brie, honey gorgonzola, or ask for a specific cheese from the aging room. Gunning for a full meal? Popular plates include the spicy pork ragu rigatoni and scallop angel hair. They also do bottomless booze for $39++ during selected windows through the week – vibes and music are always good, so this is recommended.

# This National Monument In The CBD Is Singapore’s Famous “Temple Of Love”

 By [Ng Kai](https://wonderwall.sg/search?author=Ng%20Kai&c=places--family--people--workplay--health--food)

25 September 2026

Yueh Hai Ching temple in Singapore is a [National Monument](https://wonderwall.sg/search?c=places&t=national-monuments) in the heart of Raffles Place, but it’s also famous for something less corporate: helping people find love.

While heading to One Raffles Place for a salad lunch the other day, I realised the temple was just around the corner. Now, I’m already married, so no, I wasn’t looking for divine intervention.

But I was curious: why has this nearly 200-year-old Taoist temple become such a legendary spot for singles? The answer involves an old man, goated matchmaking skills, and a whole lot of red thread.

## Overview

*   **Official name:**Yueh Hai Ching temple (粤海清庙), also known as "Wak Hai Cheng Bio" in Teochew
*   **Address:**[30B Phillip Street, Singapore 048696](https://maps.app.goo.gl/VPL5hAuwcDxuGuX66)
*   **Built:**The present-day temple was constructed in 1852-1855, but its roots can be traced back to the 1820s
*   **Current use:**Taoist temple and place of worship
*   **Year gazetted as a National Monument:**1996
*   **Nearest MRT station:**Raffles Place
*   **Admission:**Free
*   **Opening hours:**8am-5pm daily, including public holidays

## Why Yueh Hai Ching temple is worth a visit

The first thing that struck me was the contrast. Surrounded almost completely by glass-and-steel CBD skyscrapers is this ornate temple filled with incense, carved timber and colourful ceramic figures.

If you work around Raffles Place, it’s surprisingly easy to walk past without realising that one of Singapore’s oldest Chinese temples is sitting right there.

And unlike some heritage buildings that now serve completely different purposes, Yueh Hai Ching temple is still a living place of worship. People enter to pray for health, blessings and, famously, love.

![Image 7: National_Monument_Yueh_Hai_Ching_Temple_Wikipedia_Yue_Lao](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/08/national-monuments-of-singapore-yueh-hai-ching-temple/national_monument_yueh_hai_ching_temple_wikipedia_yue_lao.jpg?sfvrsn=609d8cd3_1)  
_IMAGE: WIKIMEDIA COMMONS/@SHIZHAO_

## Meet Yue Lao, the Chinese God of love and matchmaking

One reason the temple has earned its “Temple of Love” nickname is Yue Lao (月老), the Chinese deity of love and matchmaking.

His name means the “Old Man Under the Moon”; and according to Chinese folklore, Yue Lao connects people destined to be together with an invisible red thread, no matter how far apart they may be. That explains all the red strings around his shrine.

There are other temples in Singapore where Yue Lao is worshipped, but the deity here has developed a particularly strong reputation among devotees seeking relationships and marriage. Whether that comes down to destiny, faith or excellent word-of-mouth – only the successful matches will know.

## Has Yue Lao actually helped people find love?

Singles, I can't promise a lunchtime visit will have your soulmate waiting outside your office door by the end of the working day. But, there are some pretty convincing testimonials of Yue Lao's matchmaking prowess.

[In 2016](https://www.facebook.com/thengeeannkongsi/photos/a-match-made-in-heavenit-is-literally-a-match-made-in-heaven-for-34-year-old-mah/336438173355731/), Mah Chun How and Kang Say See became the first couple to solemnise their marriage here following the temple’s restoration. Both had separately prayed to Yue Lao before relatives introduced them to each other, without knowing the other had done the same. They later returned to marry at the temple on Yue Lao’s birthday.

[In 2022](https://thethaiger.com/news/world/divine-match-thai-womans-prayer-to-chinese-god-of-love-leads-to-singaporean-soulmate), Pimmada, a 23-year-old Thai woman, visited Yueh Hai Ching temple while holidaying in Singapore and prayed to Yue Lao for a partner before returning home.Two months later, she met Singaporean Yang Zi Hao, then 28, at a friend’s gathering in Thailand.

Despite a language barrier – Pimmada spoke Thai while Yang relied partly on Google Translate and basic Thai – the pair started dating and decided to marry about six months later. They subsequently returned to Singapore for their marriage registration and made another trip to the temple to offer their thanks.

So, if the usual lineup of run clubs, dating apps, and singles' mixers have borne little success for you... maybe it's time to make a wish to the Old Man Under the Moon at Yueh Hai Ching temple.

## Before Yueh Hai Ching became the “Temple of Love”

Nobody can say when the temple was first built.

Teochew immigrants originated from the Chaoshan region in South China, situated at the eastern tip of Guangdong Province. Upon arriving in Singapore in 1819 or 1820, they erected a modest shrine made of wood and _attap_ on what is now Philip Street, where they offered prayers of thanks to Mazu (妈祖), the Goddess of the Seas, for her protection during their perilous sea journeys.

This gesture gave rise to the temple’s name, which translates into English as the "Temple of the Calm Sea of the Guangdong (Yue) People"; its Teochew name is "Wak Hai Cheng Bio".

It's believed that in 1826, a man named Lin Pan (林泮) constructed a proper temple on the site of the original shrine. Like many other religious sites in Singapore, the temple also served as a social hub for newly arrived immigrants.

[The Ngee Ann Kongsi](https://thengeeannkongsi.com.sg/en/community-services/wak-hai-cheng-bio-yueh-hai-ching-temple/)took over management in 1845, and the temple was expanded between 1852 and 1855 as Singapore’s Teochew community grew.

## What to look out for when you visit Yueh Hai Ching temple

![Image 8: Yueh Hai Ching temple roof decorations](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/08/national-monuments-of-singapore-yueh-hai-ching-temple/national_monument_yueh_hai_ching_temple_roof_1.jpg?sfvrsn=69b819eb_1)

![Image 9: Yueh Hai Ching temple roof decorations](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/08/national-monuments-of-singapore-yueh-hai-ching-temple/national_monument_yueh_hai_ching_temple_roof_2.jpg?sfvrsn=70fcdff8_1)  
_IMAGES: NG KAI_

### The detailed roofs

Make sure you look up. The temple’s stunning roof decorations, including detailed depictions of dragons, were created using a traditional technique from Guangdong known as _qian ci_ (嵌瓷), more commonly referred to as _jian nian_ (剪粘), which translates to "cut and paste". This method involves carefully cutting colourful ceramic pieces into smaller shapes and arranging them into intricate mosaic designs.

Similar decorative work can also be seen on the roofs of other National Monuments in Singapore, such as the [Former House of Tan Yeok Nee](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-house-of-tan-yeok-nee), [Thian Hock Keng](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-thian-hock-keng-temple), [Former Keng Teck Whay Building](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-former-keng-teck-whay-building), [Hong San See](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-hong-san-see), and [Lian Shan Shuang Lin Monastery](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-lian-shan-shuang-lin-monastery).

![Image 10: Carving inside Yueh Hai Ching temple, a National Monument of Singapore](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/08/national-monuments-of-singapore-yueh-hai-ching-temple/national_monument_yueh_hai_ching_temple_carving_dragon.jpg?sfvrsn=159cfa44_1)

![Image 11: Carving inside Yueh Hai Ching temple, a National Monument of Singapore](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/08/national-monuments-of-singapore-yueh-hai-ching-temple/national_monument_yueh_hai_ching_temple_inside_carving_tiger.jpg?sfvrsn=106bc378_1)_IMAGES: NG KAI_

### Beautiful carvings inside the temple

Its interior is adorned with elaborate carvings that portray scenes from well-known Chinese legends and folklore, including "Eight Immortals Crossing the Seas" (八仙过海), "Ruse of the Empty City" (空城计), and "Madam White Snake Steals Lingzhi Grass to Save Xu Xian" (白素贞偷灵芝草救许仙).

![Image 12: The words on the topmost plaque were blessings from an emperor of China!](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/08/national-monuments-of-singapore-yueh-hai-ching-temple/national_monuments_yueh_hai_ching_temple_emperor.jpg?sfvrsn=b1e2ad2e_1)  
_The words on the topmost plaque were blessings from an emperor of China! | IMAGE: NG KAI_

### An imperial plaque

The temple also has a major historical flex: in 1899, Emperor Guangxu of the Qing Dynasty presented Yueh Hai Ching temple with a scroll bearing four calligraphic characters – _shu hai xiang yun_ (曙海祥云) – personally inscribed by him.

Translated as “moving seas with peaceful clouds above”, the phrase symbolised the Emperor's blessings to the Chinese community in Singapore. This honour was granted in appreciation of the temple’s donation towards flood relief efforts in Shandong, China.

The characters were later carved onto a large wooden plaque, which still hangs prominently in the temple. Apart from Yueh Hai Ching temple, [Thian Hock Keng](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-thian-hock-keng-temple) is the only other temple in Singapore known to have received a similar imperial honour.

![Image 13: Entrance and exit of Yueh Hai Ching temple, a National Monument of Singapore](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/08/national-monuments-of-singapore-yueh-hai-ching-temple/national_monument_yueh_hai_ching_temple_entrance.jpg?sfvrsn=cb5b1fb8_1)_IMAGE: NG KAI_

## Yueh Hai Ching temple today

More than two centuries after Teochew immigrants first established a shrine here, Yueh Hai Ching Temple remains an active place of worship in one of Singapore’s busiest business districts.

That was my favourite thing about visiting. Distracted during lunch hour, I found myself standing inside this National Monument connecting early immigrants, sea voyages, imperial China, centuries-old craftsmanship and devotees hoping to meet someone special.

PS: if Yue Lao does come through for you, I expect a wedding invite.

* * *

## Wait, what makes something a National Monument?

In Singapore, [National Monuments](https://wonderwall.sg/search?c=places&t=national-monuments) are buildings, structures or sites recognised for their national significance and value to our built heritage. They are gazetted by the Preservation of Sites and Monuments, a division of the National Heritage Board, which is why the title is reserved for places that carry especially important historical, architectural, social or cultural meaning.

As of 2026, Singapore has 77 National Monuments. Some are obvious landmarks, like the [Padang](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-the-padang), [St Andrew’s Cathedral](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-st-andrews-cathedral) and [Fort Siloso](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-fort-siloso). Others are places you may have walked past without a second thought, which is exactly why this series exists.

One [National Monument](https://wonderwall.sg/search?c=places&t=national-monuments) at a time, we’re here to uncover the stories hiding in plain sight.

# This National Monument Holds The Record For Singapore’s Longest Spice Line

 By [Ng Kai](https://wonderwall.sg/search?author=Ng%20Kai&c=places--family--people--workplay--health--food)

01 October 2025

What is a [National Monument](https://wonderwall.sg/search?c=places&t=national-monuments)? Who gazettes them? How many national monuments are there in Singapore? To date, the Preservation of Sites and Monuments, a division of National Heritage Board, has identified and gazetted 77 buildings, structures and sites of national significance as an integral part of Singapore’s built heritage.

And we're here to tell you all about them - one National Monument at a time!

You've probably passed by or stepped into more than a few of them without realising they were National Monuments: [Al-Abrar Mosque](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-al-abrar-mosque), [Asian Civilisations Museum](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-asian-civilisations-museum), the [Civilian War Memorial](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-civilian-war-memorial), [St Andrew's Cathedral](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-st-andrews-cathedral), the [Esplanade Park Memorials](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-esplanade-park-memorials), [Fort Siloso](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-fort-siloso) on Sentosa - no need to plan an itinerary for friends visiting from overseas; just show them this article ✌️

In this edition, we put under the magnifying glass an almost 200-year-old building that showcases Indian Muslim culture and heritage: the Former Nagore Dargah.

## 📍 Location

The Former Nagore Dargah was the 9th building to be gazetted as a National Monument, and is located near other National Monuments such as the [Former Keng Teck Whay Building](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-former-keng-teck-whay-building), [Thian Hock Keng temple](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-thian-hock-keng-temple), and [Al-Abrar Mosque](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-al-abrar-mosque). The MRT station nearest to it is Telok Ayer.

## 📅 Significant dates

### Dates built:

*   1828-1830: A shrine named "Shahul Hamid Dargah" was built
*   2007-2011: Major restoration works

### Milestones:

*   29 May 2011: The building was converted into the Nagore Dargah Indian Muslim Heritage Centre
*   January 2015: A multimedia exhibit was included inside 

**Date gazetted:**19 Nov 1974

![Image 7: Nagore Dargah in the late 19th/early 20th century.](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/09/national-monuments-of-singapore-former-nagore-dargah/national_monuments_nagore_old.jpg?sfvrsn=f679e15a_1)_Nagore Dargah in the late 19th/early 20th century. | IMAGE: WIKIMEDIA COMMONS/@ALFONS VON MUMM_

## 📜 History

Starting from the early 1820s, a minority of Indian Muslims from the Coromandel Coast in South India, known as the Chulias, began migrating to Singapore in significant numbers. Initially, their designated _kampong_ was situated elsewhere along the [Singapore River](https://wonderwall.sg/places/adventures-at-home-lets-rediscover-the-singapore-river), as laid out in Sir Stamford Raffles's 1822 Town Plan. However, over time, a substantial Indian Muslim community also settled and worked around Telok Ayer Street, which was a crucial business and residential area for the Chinese.

Between 1828 and 1830, the Chulias constructed a shrine at the intersection of Telok Ayer Street and Boon Tat Street in memory of a revered holy man named Shahul Hamid of Nagore. Originally known as Shahul Hamid Dargah, it later became known as Nagore Dargah. This shrine is a replica of the original shrine in India and does not contain any bodily relics of the holy man it is dedicated to. The shrine's construction is attributed to two brothers, Mohammed and Haja Mohideen, who transported limestone and other building materials to build it.

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZxllZ95qDLg)

The shrine was situated on land initially granted to a man named Kaderpillai, with the condition that it not be used for constructing wooden or _attap_ structures.

On 15 Jun 1893, new trustees (including Mana Mohamed, Vavena Hameed, Sayna Saiboo Ghanny, Kavena Mohamed Ismail, and Tana Chinny Tamby) took over the Nagore Dargah properties through a court order.

By 1910, these trustees had either passed away or left Singapore, leading to the appointment of new trustees, namely K. Mohamed Eusope, Thambyappa Rarooter, S. Kanisah Maricayar, V. M. Kader Bux, and J. Sultan Abdul Kader, by another court order issued on 21 Nov 1910.

These trustees also oversaw the nearby [Al-Abrar Mosque](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-al-abrar-mosque) on Telok Ayer Street and the [Jamae Mosque](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-jamae-mosque) on South Bridge Road.

![Image 8: Nagore Dargah is currently managed by the Majlis Ugama Islam Singapura (MUIS).](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/09/national-monuments-of-singapore-former-nagore-dargah/nagore_dargah_entrance_2.jpg?sfvrsn=3e1c8155_1)_IMAGE: NG KAI_

Nagore Dargah is currently managed by the Majlis Ugama Islam Singapura (MUIS). Reflecting the religious and cultural diversity of early Singapore, Nagore Dargah is located on the same street as [Thian Hock Keng temple](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-thian-hock-keng-temple) (Singapore's oldest Hokkien temple) and [Al-Abrar Mosque](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-al-abrar-mosque), both gazetted National Monuments.

In the 1990s, the shrine was boarded up and closed to the public due to concerns about its structural integrity. Major restoration work was carried out in 2007, after which the building remained closed to visitors. In December 2010, MUIS announced that the building would be converted into the Nagore Dargah Indian Muslim Heritage Centre, and would feature exhibits and artefacts from the Indian Muslim community.

![Image 9: On 29 May 2011, the Nagore Dargah Indian Muslim Heritage Centre was officially inaugurated by then-President S R Nathan.](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/09/national-monuments-of-singapore-former-nagore-dargah/national_monuments_nagore_exhibit.jpg?sfvrsn=6d4834a9_1)_IMAGE: NG KAI_

On 29 May 2011, the Nagore Dargah Indian Muslim Heritage Centre was officially inaugurated by then-President S R Nathan. However, the centre had to close again in 2013 for renovations and restoration work to address issues like disintegrated wall paint due to dampness.

The centre reopened in November 2014 and introduced a new gallery in January 2015, featuring a multimedia exhibit and storyboard showcasing pioneers of the Indian Muslim community in Singapore.

* * *

![Image 10: According to the Singapore Book of Records, a 36.2m long spice line was unveiled on 26 Oct 2019 at the Former Nagore Dargah.](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/09/national-monuments-of-singapore-former-nagore-dargah/national_monuments_nagore_record.jpg?sfvrsn=72714b94_1)  
_IMAGE: NG KAI_

According to the [Singapore Book of Records](https://singaporerecords.com/longest-spice-line/), a 36.2m long spice line was unveiled on 26 Oct 2019 at the Former Nagore Dargah. This was due to Singapore's past as a vital entrepôt:

_About 200 years ago, Singapore became an important entrepot largely because of the demand for spices from western countries. Many of the early Indian Muslims were spice traders. Hence Nagore Dargah Indian Muslim Heritage Centre decided to display a collection of 80 different spices forming a 36.2m spice line on its wall. About 410 bottles were used for the line. It was officially opened on 26 Oct 2019._

![Image 11: The Former Nagore Dargah is designed in an eclectic architectural style that incorporates elements, such as fluted (ridged) Corinthian and Doric pilasters (rectangular columns) on its facades.](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/09/national-monuments-of-singapore-former-nagore-dargah/national_monuments_nagore_design.jpg?sfvrsn=1e411c7_1)  
_IMAGE: NG KAI_

![Image 12: The Former Nagore Dargah is designed in an eclectic architectural style that incorporates elements, such as Doric columns and arches in the interior.](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/09/national-monuments-of-singapore-former-nagore-dargah/national_monuments_nagore_interior.jpg?sfvrsn=e32d2458_1)_IMAGE: NG KAI_

## 📐 Design and architecture

The Former Nagore Dargah is designed in an eclectic architectural style that incorporates elements from various traditions. In addition to the minarets (the tower from which the faithful are called to prayer five times each day by a _muezzin_, or crier) and crescent-and-star motifs commonly found in mosques, the building features fluted (ridged) Corinthian and Doric pilasters (rectangular columns) on its façades, along with Doric columns and arches in the interior.

![Image 13: Large French-style windows with semi-circular fanlights grace the wall facing Boon Tat Street, ensuring effective ventilation and a comfortable interior climate.](https://wonderwall.sg/images/default-source/content/dam/wonderwall/images/2023/09/national-monuments-of-singapore-former-nagore-dargah/nagore_dargah_side_1.jpg?sfvrsn=2098336f_1)_IMAGE: NG KAI_

Large French-style windows with semi-circular fanlights grace the wall facing Boon Tat Street, ensuring effective ventilation and a comfortable interior climate.

Much like [Al-Abrar Mosque](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-al-abrar-mosque), [Jamae Mosque](https://wonderwall.sg/places/national-monuments-of-singapore-jamae-mosque), and the memorial shrines in Nagore and [Penang](https://wonderwall.sg/places/penang-rewritten-what-do-the-citys-new-hotels-say-about-its-second-act), the most distinctive feature of the Former Nagore Dargah's front façade is its two square minaret-like towers that extend above the building's flat roof. These towers are adorned with niches (cavities in the wall), which were originally used to hold oil lamps during certain religious festivals. A complex miniature palace façade, featuring numerous perforations with various designs representing doorways and windows, connects these towers.

The main entrance of the building is distinguished by a Moorish multi-foliated arch, and decorative mouldings of flowers and leaves adorn the façade wall.

## 🕖 Opening hours

Regular visiting hours are:

*   10am to 5.30pm, Monday to Friday
*   9am to 1pm,Saturdays

The building is closed on Sundays.

## 🎟️ Admission

Entry is free.

## Unique heritage trails in Singapore

### [Ang Mo Kio Heritage Trail](https://www.roots.gov.sg/places/places-landing/trails/ang-mo-kio-heritage-trail)

[![Image 5: Ang Mo Kio Heritage Trail](https://media.timeout.com/images/106049084/750/422/image.jpg) ![Image 6: Ang Mo Kio Heritage Trail](https://media.timeout.com/images/106049084/750/562/image.jpg) Photograph: National Heritage Board](https://www.roots.gov.sg/places/places-landing/trails/ang-mo-kio-heritage-trail)

Explore the rich [heritage of Ang Mo Kio](https://www.timeout.com/singapore/news/rediscover-the-neighbourhood-of-ang-mo-kio-through-this-renewed-heritage-trail-092823) by visiting 40 heritage sites, including 10 prominent heritage markers. Additionally, the revamped trail provides you with the option to embark on three distinct themed routes tailored to your preferences: _Iconic Landmarks_ highlights the town's iconic buildings and sites, _Hidden Heartland Gems_ uncovers overlooked treasures, and _Scenic Fringes_ offers insights into the district's lesser-known outskirts.

**TOUR** Discover hidden landmarks in Ang Mo Kio, including the Church of Christ the King, the area's inaugural and only Catholic church. Explore three temples with historical roots in the region's former villages: _Gao Lin Gong, Kim Eang Tong,_ and _Leng San Giam_. The trail also unveils lesser-known narratives, such as a concealed assortment of artworks by the Chinese artist Xu Beihong, once housed at Chong Boon Chinese School in Lelong Pah. Noteworthy sites also include the _Kebun Baru Birdsinging Club_, Singapore's largest bird singing and display arena boasting 1,000 cages.

[Read more](https://www.roots.gov.sg/places/places-landing/trails/ang-mo-kio-heritage-trail)
